Around the Horn (28th episode) If this were an old-school procedural, 28 episodes would put us at season 2. If we consider this exercise to be more akin to a prestige drama from the present-day TV landscape, we might already be on season 5. Let’s go back around the horn. This is our 28th roundup of articles on China’s AI ecosystem. For new readers, here’s how it works (see ChinAI #376 for the previous edition): I give short previews of ten articles that caught my eye during a scan through my usual sources (all published within the past week or so). The title for each preview links to the original article in Chinese. Readers vote on next week’s feature translation by replying to the email and/or commenting on the post with the number of your preferred article. *Extra weight goes to votes from those of you who support ChinAI through a paid subscription. The main idea is that any of these 10 links would have made for a great feature translation this week — like the The Lowdown tv show’s soundtrack, there are no skips! 1) The final struggles of a batch of near-death robotics companies Summary: In the last two years, ~30 robotics manufacturers (many of them Chinese) have faced severe operational crises. This piece digs into why some companies are struggling for their last gasps. Source: 虎嗅 (Huxiu), a well-known platform that shares user-generated content but also publishes their own pieces on China’s science and technology ecosystem. 2) I ’m not that optimistic about BAT doing Personal Agents Summary: As Meta’s Muse and Spear Street Technology’s Instinct have taken off, China’s big tech giants position themselves to develop their own breakthrough Personal Agent. However, this author sees various barriers, with computing power at the top of the list: Since a personal agent has to remain active, retain context, and execute long-running tasks, it is token-hungry. Given China’s strain on computing resources, “ Every unit of compute allocated to a personal agent is one less unit available for other purposes .” Includes this interesting anecdote: “ An insider revealed that last year, when Tencent faced an acute shortage of computing power, it rented a significant number of GPUs from another major tech firm. Feature Translation: The 2026 VC sphere is defying common sense Context: Liu Xiaoqing is director of analysis at IT Juzi [IT桔子], one of my favorite sources on China’s venture capital ecosystem. Last week, she posted a lengthy denunciation that begins with this bold statement: ' In 2026, a year where “embodied AI” has become practically in unison with “Chinese venture capital,” there are too many things happening that run counter to common sense . Key Takeaways: Let’s break down Liu’s critique into five main parts: 1) Inflated valuations based on resumes alone: big tech execs and elite university PhD graduates easily land initial valuations of hundreds of millions of RMB Liu critiques the restless, rushed mindset of these young geniuses, who spin and chase narratives defined by fundraising windows — unmoored from technological progress and maturity. 2) Hastily assembled all-star lineups that don’t form real teams. Liu has seen countless founding teams that look good on paper: “ a brilliant technical lead, a former executive from a major tech firm, a supply-chain veteran, and someone well-versed in the world of capital.” In practice, whole is much less than the sum of its parts. In a piece full of zingers, this might have been my favorite one: Yet, for many teams today, the journey looks more like this: the first time you meet happens at a dinner arranged by a financial advisor, the second time you meet takes place at the negotiating table for a term sheet, and the third you meet is the signing ceremony. People with completely different backgrounds, splitting equity 40/30/30, suddenly find themselves “running a company together” from day one. That’s not called a partnership; that’s called assembling a party for a video game quest. 3) Startups look too much like big tech giants from day one. Liu recalls learning about an embodied AI startup founded in 2023. Its founding experience reflects how the VC market is skipping steps when it comes to cultivating organizational capital: They had raised hundreds of millions in their Series A round. Their office was in a high-rise building, complete with a logo wall at the reception. They had hired an HR director poached from a major tech giant, who spent the very first month setting up a rigid corporate hierarchy and performance review system. content: ChinAI #380: It’s getting more and more difficult to make money ChinAI Newsletter Subscribe Sign in ChinAI #380: It’s getting more and more difficult to make money Jeffrey Ding Nov 02, 2026 12 1 3 Share Greetings from a world where… perhaps it could still be the Hawkeyes football team’s year …As always, the searchable archive of all past issues is here . Please please subscribe here to support ChinAI under a Guardian /Wikipedia-style tipping model (everyone gets the same content but those who can pay support access for all AND compensation for awesome ChinAI contributors). Feature Translation: Why is it becoming more and more difficult to make money? The most profound analysis I’ve read Context: This week’s essay comes from budongjing [不懂经] , a platform that often translates English-language books on financial and economic issues (e.g., Naval Ravikant’s HOW TO GET RICH: (without getting lucky) . I came across this post after it got aggregated by Huxiu, a popular science and tech news platform, where it accumulated 100k+ views. Key Takeaways: The vibes of China’s economy summed up in one sentence? “It’s getting more and more difficult to make money.” The author writes, “ Over the past two decades, you didn’t need to be super talented. You just needed courage, a willingness to grind over and over again, and you could take flight by standing at the window of opportunity. Real estate, the internet, and foreign trade—these three great engines of wealth creation took turns driving prosperity. Now, however, these engines have slowed down; we have entered an era of ‘zero-sum’ competition .” The budongjing essay fleshes out the vibes with these vignettes: “ In the ‘This Work Thing [上班这件事]’ Douban group, it is the late-night sigh of a 35-year-old tech-giant employee, laid off and left to grapple with mortgage and car loan payments. On Xiaohongshu, it is the experience of a young professional in Shanghai, earning 8,000 yuan a month, who managed to secure a shred of financial security by practicing extreme fragility. On Weibo, it is the story of a small-business owner, forced to close shop after orders plummeted in the post-pandemic era.” Budongjing traces the cause of this feeling of economic malaise to a structural shift in the Chinese economy from “arranging atoms” to “arranging bits”, largely adapting the views of Emad Mostaque’s book The Last Economy . The old paradigm tried to manufacture scarcity; in the digital realm, instead of trying to abuse software patents and guard closed systems, the new paradigm favors open-source networks that achieve exponential scale. One interesting takeaway (which I disagree with, but it’s notable that this is how some Chinese bloggers are translating these structural changes into self-help advice to individuals): “ The old narrative that ‘you can succeed if you just work hard’ is being supplanted by a harsh topology where ‘connections matter more than effort.’ ” Highlighting AI as the ultimate shock that will perform ne

content: Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI - by Ethan Mollick One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI General, often expert, and sometimes jagged Ethan Mollick Nov 09, 2026 1,477 239 175 Share Before getting started, I wanted to thank my readers for making my new book, Co-Existence, a New York Times bestseller two weeks in a row. If you haven’t read it, you can get a copy here . I have had the chance to use the new Claude Fable 5.2 quite a bit before its public launch 1 , and it is very impressive, following on the already excellent Opus 5.5. AI has gotten so good, in fact, that it is worth asking if Anthropic’s newest models (and the inevitable competing models OpenAI and Google will soon release) cross the boundary into being an Artificial General Intelligence? AGI is a much-debated term with a lot of potential definitions. For this post, I’ll go with: “an AI as good as most human experts at most intellectual tasks you can do with a computer.” This explicitly excludes a lot of human work, including interacting with the physical world and other people, as well as most actual jobs, where “using a computer” is just one task among many. Still, even with these caveats, building a limited form of AGI has long been the goal of AI developers. So as not to keep you in suspense, I think the answer is that this is “almost” AGI, or what I have called Jagged AGI. Even within my limited definition, there are still important areas in many tasks where AI is jagged enough to fall well behind human capability. But the jaggedness is no longer about simple errors or hallucinations, which makes it harder to describe. So I want to try to do that in this post by showing you what Fable can do and where the gaps are. To get started I asked the new model: “I write OneUsefulThing among other stuff, I need you to create the most impressive thing I can share with people when you launch. It needs to be embeddable in a post and i can preface it however you like. it needs to have a visceral impact on people to show what you can do and the range of capabilities. It should grab them quickly. Be amazingly clever about this.” Fable asked me not to reveal anything until you had watched its video to the end. This was in one shot, with no feedback from me beyond the prompt. There is creativity here (including in the twist ending) and judgment and playfulness and cleverness. This is, I think, at the level of a human expert trying to make a movie with code alone, the sort of performance I would once have associated with AGI. The “G” in AGI Code and video creation have been areas where AI development has focused, so is Fable 5.2 really a General Intelligence? summary: My second book on AI, Co-Existence, is out today (and you can get it here ), 30 months after the release of Co-Intelligence in early 2024. Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite love...
content: 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts) - by Ethan Mollick One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts) My new book is out today... what happened since the last one Ethan Mollick Oct 20, 2026 819 148 70 Share My second book on AI, Co-Existence, is out today (and you can get it here ), 30 months after the release of Co-Intelligence in early 2024. Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite lovely charts. Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence , I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence , I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single “orchestrator” agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes. And since I didn’t have to do the work, I had the AI make many options for me. I picked some and gave handwavy reactions to others that would drive a human team mad (“make it better”). It even caught that I’d gotten the math wrong. I was going to call this post “28 months on the exponential.” Some examples of interacting with Claude to make the graphics for this post. Notice that it corrected me. “This is the worst AI you will ever use” I wrote this in my last book on AI, and it has continued to be literally true at every moment since. From early 2023 through early 2024, there was a single AI model that was undeniably the best in the world: GPT-4 from OpenAI. This was the AI model that most people remember from the first couple years of AI use, it was the one I thought about while writing Co-Intelligence , and it was the one that gave ChatGPT its status as the default AI for many people. Since then, twenty different AI models have held the lead at one time or another, all from Anthropic, Google, or OpenAI. Which company had the best AI model in the world. But the changing lead alone hides an even bigger change. A total of 180 AI models are now better than GPT-4 was at its release, many of which are open weights models, which anyone is free to use or modify. Nineteen of them can run on a modern smartphone. We are living in an exponential The data below draws on the METR Long Horizon Benchmark, which used to be the most famous chart in AI. title: <![CDATA[The Dot and the Swarm]]>
summary: I generally think I have done a good job anticipating the direction and pace of AI over the few years I have been writing this Substack, but I think I recently got something fairly large wrong. In the last year I have been posting about how I suspected that humans would have to approach working with...
content: The Dot and the Swarm - by Ethan Mollick - One Useful Thing One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in The Dot and the Swarm Benefitting from the Bitter Lesson Ethan Mollick Oct 01, 2026 1,407 236 144 Share I generally think I have done a good job anticipating the direction and pace of AI over the few years I have been writing this Substack, but I think I recently got something fairly large wrong. In the last year I have been posting about how I suspected that humans would have to approach working with agents as a manager, deciding how to delegate work to agents and specifying how those agents should be organized. I thought that getting agents to work effectively as a group would take careful construction, akin to building a company, and that this would take time to figure out. Nope. I fell prey to The Bitter Lesson, the hard truth, learned over and over again, that things that we thought required elaborate human rules and thinking can be solved with the brute force of better machine learning systems and more AI. The Bitter Lesson is everywhere among AI startups and companies adopting AI. A huge amount of effort went into building elaborate computer systems to feed AIs the right information at the right time, but AI systems have learned to seek out information themselves. The same thing happened to prompting. People built elaborate templates and chains of prompts that walked the AI through a task one step at a time. Then newer models turned out to be better at planning the steps themselves, and, as our research shows , planning steps have much less value. The history of the Bitter Le— — you know what? I don’t really need to explain the Bitter Lesson, I asked Claude to do it in a music video. With one prompt, Fable wrote the lyrics and submitted it to Suno; Opus 5.5 did everything else using code alone without any image generation (How did Opus 5.5 pull this off? The Bitter Lesson tells you!). I gave no feedback at all. As somebody who teaches managers and has published research on management, I guess I believed that managing agents would be different. Humans have been working on management for a very long time without fully figuring it out. It seemed like the kind of thing that would need to be designed by people, at least for a while. It turns out that organizing work is just one more thing AI can learn to do. Which brings us to dots and Muse. Dots and Muse The number one app in the App Store right now is Meta’s Muse, a personal agent that promises to do work for you. OpenAI has now released a competitor tool, called dots. They aren’t alone: SpaceX’s Grok Bot, Instinct, and Gemini Spark all do similar things, more or less. All of these agents draw inspiration from a phenomenon you might remember from earlier this year, OpenClaw. The idea of OpenClaw and its successors, which I will call Clawlikes, is that they give an AI agent access to a computer and connect to your accounts (emails, financial records, etc.). content: My wife thinks AI is a person - Ben's Bites Ben’s Bites Subscribe Sign in My wife thinks AI is a person which isn’t as nuts as it sounds... Nov 19, 2026 43 Share The other day my wife was chatting with AI. P.s. The full interactive version of this post is here . So let’s overlook the actual impossibilities and find out. Before we do the maths, people have been trying versions of this for 256 years. Nearly all of them shut down or got caught. None of them came close to today’s scale. So what would it actually take? Let’s be generous. Assume everyone types at world-record speed, 200 words a minute, non-stop. Everyone is happy to wait 10 minutes for a reply. And it’s a remote company spread across every time zone, so someone is always awake. The average ChatGPT user sends about 4 messages a day, and a reply is roughly 500 words now. With over a billion people using the big AI chatbots, that’s about 6 billion messages every day. 10.4 million people typing at world-record speed, round the clock, with no sleep, no lunch, and no days off. Okay, let’s run it like a real company instead. Which means it needs a CEO. Me. 11.8 billion internal messages a day, just to keep the place running. Oh, and we still have to answer the 6 billion messages people actually sent us. All in, you’d need 77.4 million staff just to keep 10.4 million people typing at any given moment. If you want to check my maths: a 40-hour week, time off from a 2025 survey of UK call centres , 12.1 people per manager ( the US average ), and 2 HR people per 100 staff ( SHRM ). People quit at the US rate , earn the US median for customer service , and get 153 chat messages a day , like the average Microsoft Teams user. The biggest Zoom call holds 1 million . More people won’t work. But what about a guessing game from 1950, played by a mathematician called Claude Shannon? Yes, Claude. He picked a line from a book, hid it from his wife Betty, and got her to guess it one letter at a time. Betty didn’t know the sentence, she just knew the patterns of English. My wife does this to me every day. She’s had years of practice. So what if we replaced Betty with a computer? For more than 60 years, the answer was no. Giving machines more to read barely helped, because they could only see the last couple of words. Try guessing what comes after “speak fluent…” with no other clues. In 2017, eight people at Google let it see every word at once and weigh the ones that matter, like France. They called that attention, and the machine a transformer. It’s the T in ChatGPT. Suddenly, giving it more to read actually worked. More text, bigger brain, better guesses. Writing a reply is the same thing. It reads what you said and guesses the next word, or piece of a word (called a token), sticks it on the end, looks back at everything again, and guesses the next one. It’s read websites, books, forums, fan wikis, and code. A top model trains on more than 32 trillion tokens. Reading that non-stop would take you about 190,0
